sentences.text: Beishanlong is the second-largest known ornithomimosaur, surpassed in size only by Deinocheirus. The genus name combines Chinese words for "North Mountains" and "dragon", while the species name grandis means "large" in Latin.

This animal possessed long arms and legs but lacked the extremely elongated hands, feet, and claws found in later ornithomimosaurs. Instead, it had strong forelimbs with fifteen-centimeter-long claws likely excellent for raking or digging the ground.

The holotype subadult individual is estimated to be between 5.9 and 7 meters long and weigh between 375 and 626 kilograms. Since this specimen was about 7 meters long and weighed 600 kilograms as a subadult nearing fourteen years old, adults could reach 8 meters and 750 kilograms.

The holotype specimen FRDC-GS GJ (06) 01-18 was found in 2006 and consists of a partial skeleton lacking the skull. Paratypes include two specimens found in 2007: one with hindlimb remains and another consisting of a pair of pubis bones. A fourth fossil found in 1999, IVPP V12756 consisting of foot bones, was tentatively referred to the species.

The type species Beishanlong grandis was named online in 2009 and formally published in January 2010 by a team including Peter Makovicky, Li Daiqing, Gao Keqin, Matthew Lewin, Gregory Erickson, and Mark Norrell.

Histological analysis indicates the holotype individual of Beishanlong was still growing when it died, despite being one of the largest definitive ornithomimosaurs described. A histological study of the fibula found thirteen or fourteen growth lines, indicating the individual was subadult but growth had already slowed.

The original describers assigned Beishanlong to Ornithomimosauria in a basal position. In 2014, Yuong-Nam Lee et al. recovered Beishanlong as a member of Deinocheiridae, basal to a clade containing Garudimimus and Deinocheirus.

Beishanlong shared territory with Therizinosaurus, Suzhousaurus, and the oviraptorosaurian Gigantoraptor, providing evidence for parallel evolution of gigantism in separate ceratosaurian lineages with beaks and possibly herbivorous diets in a brief period in Central Asia.

Beishanlong lived during the late Aptian stage, with fossils found in the Xiagou Formation of the Xinminpu Group. Beishanlong lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 115 to 100 million years ago, between the Aptian and Albian stages in what is now Asia. The time range for Beishanlong is estimated from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago.
